lessons.title: Context Clues and Word Meaning
lessons.learningGoal: Students will use nearby words, examples, contrasts, and explanations to figure out unfamiliar words.
successCriteria: I can use clues in a sentence to choose a likely word meaning.
I can tell whether a clue gives an example, contrast, or explanation.
I can check whether a word meaning makes sense in the whole sentence.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise using context clues to infer word meaning in grade-level sentences.
lessonContent: Context clues are hints around an unfamiliar word that help the reader work out a likely meaning.
A definition or explanation clue tells the meaning directly, often in the same sentence.
An example clue gives one or more examples that help narrow the meaning.
A contrast clue uses words such as but, unlike, although, or however to show an opposite or different idea.
A careful reader checks the possible meaning in the whole sentence before choosing an answer.

studentActivity.title: Context Clue Detective
studentActivity.mission: Use clues in sentences to figure out precise word meanings.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: use nearby clues
steps.text: When you meet an unfamiliar word, do not guess too quickly. Read the words around it. A sentence may give an explanation, example, or contrast that helps you choose a meaning that fits.

steps.title: How Context Clues Work
steps.prompt: Look for the kind of clue
steps.text: Some sentences explain the word directly: 'The fabric was transparent, or easy to see through.' Some give examples: 'nocturnal animals, such as owls and bats.' Some use contrast: 'Unlike the noisy hall, the room was tranquil.' First find the clue, then choose the meaning that fits the whole sentence.

steps.title: Explanation Clue
steps.prompt: The guide was cautious, moving slowly and checking the trail before each step. What does cautious most likely mean?
steps.feedback: Correct. Moving slowly and checking the trail shows careful behaviour.
steps.hint: Look at what the guide is doing.

steps.title: Example Clue
steps.prompt: Many nocturnal animals, such as owls and bats, are active at night. Which clue helps explain nocturnal?
choices: owls and bats are active at night
steps.correctAnswer: owls and bats are active at night
steps.feedback: Yes. The examples point to animals that are active at night.
steps.hint: The examples tell what kind of animals they are.

steps.title: Contrast Clue
steps.prompt: Unlike the noisy hallway, the library was tranquil. What does tranquil most likely mean?
steps.feedback: Correct. Unlike noisy tells you tranquil means almost the opposite.
steps.hint: The word unlike gives a contrast.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A context clue can appear after the unfamiliar word.
steps.feedback: Correct. Clues can come before or after the word.
steps.hint: Readers should check the whole sentence.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised finding clues around unfamiliar words.

steps.title: Check the Whole Sentence
steps.prompt: A meaning must fit
steps.text: A word meaning has to fit the whole sentence, not just one nearby word. If two choices seem possible, reread and ask which one makes the sentence clearer and more exact.

steps.title: Choose the Meaning
steps.prompt: The student revised her paragraph to make the explanation more precise. What does precise most likely mean?
steps.feedback: Yes. A revised explanation should become more exact and clear.
steps.hint: Think about what revision should improve.

steps.title: Multiple Clues
steps.prompt: The instructions were mandatory; everyone had to follow them before using the equipment. What does mandatory mean?
steps.feedback: Correct. Everyone had to follow them is the clue.
steps.hint: Had to follow is the strongest clue.

steps.title: Best Fit
steps.prompt: The old bridge was sturdy enough to hold the loaded cart. Which meaning best fits sturdy?
steps.feedback: Correct. Holding a loaded cart points to strength.
steps.hint: Ask what quality helps a bridge hold weight.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: If a meaning does not fit the sentence, a careful reader should try another meaning.
steps.feedback: Correct. The meaning should make sense in context.
steps.hint: Context is how you check the choice.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing meanings that fit the context.

quiz.title: Context Clues and Word Meaning Quiz

questions.prompt: The path was narrow, barely wide enough for one person. What does narrow mean?
questions.reviewNote: Barely wide enough is the clue.

questions.prompt: Aquatic plants, including water lilies and pondweed, grow in water. What does aquatic mean?
The first draft was vague, but the final draft was specific. What does vague most likely mean?
The class collaborated, sharing ideas and dividing the work fairly. What does collaborated mean?
questions.reviewNote: Sharing ideas and dividing work point to working together.

questions.type: A contrast clue often uses words such as but, unlike, or however.
The first meaning that pops into your mind is always the best meaning.
questions.correctAnswer: A reader should check the context.

questions.prompt: The puppy was reluctant to enter the cold water and backed away from the shore. What does reluctant mean?
Which habit best helps with context clues?
choices: Reread the sentence and check which meaning fits.
Choose the longest definition every time.
questions.correctAnswer: Reread the sentence and check which meaning fits.
questions.reviewNote: The meaning must fit the sentence.

lessons.title: Prefixes, Suffixes, and Roots
lessons.learningGoal: Students will use prefixes, suffixes, and roots to understand and build words.
successCriteria: I can identify common prefixes and suffixes.
I can use word parts to make a reasonable meaning.
I can check a word-part meaning against the sentence.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise using word parts to understand meanings without treating word parts as shortcuts that replace context.
lessonContent: A prefix is added to the beginning of a base word and changes the meaning.
A suffix is added to the end of a word and can change the meaning or the word's job in a sentence.
The base word or root carries the main meaning, but the sentence still helps confirm the meaning.
Common prefixes include re-, un-, pre-, and mis-. Common suffixes include -ful, -less, -ness, and -ly.
Students should break a word into parts, build a possible meaning, then check whether that meaning fits the sentence.

studentActivity.title: Word Parts Builder
studentActivity.mission: Break words into useful parts and use those parts to understand meaning.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: word parts carry meaning
steps.text: Many English words have parts that help with meaning. The prefix re- often means again. The prefix un- often means not. The suffix -ful can mean full of, and -less can mean without.

steps.title: How to Break a Word
steps.prompt: Find the base word first
steps.text: Start by finding the main word inside. In unhappy, happy is the base word and un- changes it to not happy. In careful, care is the base word and -ful means full of. Word parts give strong clues, but always reread the sentence to make sure the meaning works.

steps.title: Prefix Meaning
steps.prompt: In the word reread, what does re- mean?
steps.feedback: Correct. Reread means read again.
steps.hint: Think of redo or replay.

steps.title: Prefix Meaning
steps.prompt: In the word unfair, what does un- mean?
steps.feedback: Yes. Unfair means not fair.
steps.hint: Un- often changes a word to its opposite.

steps.title: Suffix Meaning
steps.prompt: Which word means full of hope?
steps.feedback: Correct. -ful can mean full of.
steps.hint: Look for the suffix that means full of.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A suffix is added to the end of a word.
steps.feedback: Correct. Suffixes come at the end.
steps.hint: Prefix begins; suffix ends.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised common prefixes and suffixes.

steps.title: Use the Sentence Too
steps.prompt: Word parts help, but context matters
steps.text: Word parts give clues, but the sentence still matters. A careful reader uses both: the word parts and the sentence around the word.

steps.title: Choose the Meaning
steps.prompt: The directions were unclear, so the group reread them. What does reread mean here?
steps.feedback: Correct. Re- and the sentence both point to reading again.
steps.hint: The group needed another look.

steps.title: Suffix Choice
steps.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence: The cracked cup was ____ for carrying water.
steps.feedback: Yes. A cracked cup would be without use for carrying water.
steps.hint: Think about whether it can do the job.

steps.title: Root Word
steps.prompt: What is the base word in disagreement?
steps.feedback: Correct. Dis- and -ment are added around agree.
steps.hint: Find the main word inside.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Word parts are helpful clues, but the sentence should still make sense.
steps.feedback: Correct. Context helps confirm the meaning.
steps.hint: Good readers use more than one clue.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using word parts and context together.

questions.prompt: What does the prefix pre- usually mean in preview?
What does mis- usually mean in misplace?
Which word means without care?
Which word names the state of being kind?
questions.reviewNote: -ness can name a quality or state.

questions.prompt: What is the base word in repainting?
The team had to reorganize the supplies after the boxes fell. What does reorganize mean?
questions.reviewNote: Re- means again, and the sentence supports it.

questions.type: A prefix is added to the beginning of a word.
questions.correctAnswer: Prefixes come before the base word.

questions.type: Word parts always give the full meaning without needing the sentence.

lessons.title: Parts of Speech in Sentences
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify how nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, and prepositions work in sentences.
successCriteria: I can identify the job a word is doing in a sentence.
I can choose words that make the sentence clearer.
I can notice how parts of speech work together.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students review parts of speech by focusing on how words function inside sentences.
lessonContent: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. A pronoun can stand in for a noun.
A verb shows action or being and tells what the subject does or is.
An adjective describes a noun by telling what kind, which one, or how many.
An adverb often describes a verb by telling how, when, where, or how much.
A preposition shows a relationship, often location or direction, such as under, beside, through, or before.
The same word can sometimes do different jobs, so students should look at how the word is used in the sentence.

Use the lesson quiz as a scored check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Language lesson.

studentActivityPlan.description: Identify the job each word is doing inside a sentence.

quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.

studentActivity.title: Sentence Word Jobs
studentActivity.mission: Identify the job each word is doing inside a sentence.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: words have jobs
steps.text: The same word can sometimes do different jobs, so pay attention to the sentence. In 'The light is bright,' light is a noun. In 'Please light the candle,' light is a verb.

steps.title: How to Test a Word
steps.prompt: Ask what job the word is doing
steps.text: To find a noun, ask who or what the sentence is about. To find a verb, ask what happens or what something is. To find an adjective, ask what kind. To find an adverb, ask how, when, where, or how much. To find a preposition, look for a word that shows a relationship, such as beside, under, after, or through.

steps.title: Find the Verb
steps.prompt: In the sentence 'The canoe drifted across the quiet lake,' which word is the verb?
steps.feedback: Correct. Drifted shows the action.
steps.hint: Ask what the canoe did.

steps.title: Find the Adjective
steps.prompt: In 'The careful artist mixed blue paint,' which word is an adjective?
steps.feedback: Yes. Careful describes the artist.
steps.hint: Adjectives describe nouns.

steps.title: Find the Adverb
steps.prompt: In 'Maya answered politely,' which word is an adverb?
steps.feedback: Correct. Politely describes how Maya answered.
steps.hint: Adverbs often tell how an action happened.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A pronoun can replace a noun to avoid repeating the same name too often.
steps.feedback: Correct. Pronouns such as she, he, they, and it can replace nouns.
steps.hint: Pronouns stand in for nouns.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying word jobs.

steps.title: Words Work Together
steps.prompt: Choose precise words
steps.text: Grammar is not only labelling words. It helps writers make meaning clear. Choose nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs that fit the exact idea.

steps.title: Precise Verb
steps.prompt: Which verb makes the sentence most precise? 'The rabbit ____ under the fence.'
steps.feedback: Yes. Darted gives a clearer action than went.
steps.hint: Choose the verb that shows a specific action.

steps.title: Pronoun Clarity
steps.prompt: Which sentence uses a pronoun most clearly?
choices: After Sara thanked Lily, Sara packed her bag.
After Sara thanked Lily, she packed her bag.
After Sara thanked Lily, they packed it.
steps.correctAnswer: After Sara thanked Lily, Sara packed her bag.
steps.feedback: Correct. Repeating Sara avoids confusion about who packed the bag.
steps.hint: Sometimes a noun is clearer than a pronoun.

steps.title: Preposition
steps.prompt: Which word shows the relationship in 'The notebook is under the desk'?
steps.feedback: Correct. Under shows where the notebook is.
steps.hint: Prepositions often tell where or when.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A precise verb can make writing clearer than a general verb.
steps.feedback: Correct. Precise verbs help readers picture the action.
steps.hint: Think of sprinted instead of went.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using parts of speech for clear meaning.

quiz.title: Parts of Speech in Sentences Quiz

questions.prompt: In 'The thunder rumbled above the valley,' which word is the verb?
In 'Kindness matters in a classroom,' which word names an idea?
Which word is an adjective in 'The narrow path curved sharply'?
Which word is an adverb in 'The team worked steadily'?
Which word is a pronoun?
Which word is a preposition in 'The keys are beside the lamp'?

questions.type: A word's job depends on how it is used in the sentence.

questions.prompt: Which verb is most precise?

lessons.title: Complete Sentences, Fragments, and Run-Ons
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify complete sentences, fragments, and run-ons and choose effective corrections.
successCriteria: I can tell whether a sentence has a subject and predicate.
I can correct fragments by adding missing information.
I can correct run-ons with punctuation or joining words.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise recognizing sentence boundaries and correcting common sentence errors.
lessonContent: A complete sentence has a subject and a predicate and expresses a complete thought.
The subject tells who or what the sentence is about. The predicate tells what the subject does or is.
A fragment is an incomplete sentence. It may be missing a subject, a predicate, or the rest of the thought.
A run-on happens when two complete thoughts are pushed together without correct punctuation or a joining word.
A writer can fix sentence problems by adding missing information, using a period, or joining ideas correctly.

Use the lesson quiz as a scored check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Language lesson.

quizPlan.title: Complete Sentences, Fragments, and Run-Ons Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Sentence completeness, fragments, run-ons, and corrections

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided practice and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Sentence Fixer
studentActivity.mission: Choose complete sentences and fix fragments and run-ons.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: complete thoughts
steps.text: A complete sentence needs someone or something the sentence is about, plus what that subject does or is. A fragment may sound like it begins an idea but does not finish it.

steps.title: Subject and Predicate
steps.prompt: Check both parts
steps.text: Ask two questions: Who or what is the sentence about? What does that subject do or what is true about it? 'The lantern glowed' is complete because lantern is the subject and glowed tells what happened. 'After the lantern glowed' is a fragment because the word after starts an idea that needs more information.

steps.title: Complete Sentence
steps.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
choices: The maple leaves turned red in October.
steps.correctAnswer: The maple leaves turned red in October.
steps.feedback: Correct. It has a subject and tells what happened.
steps.hint: Find the choice that gives a complete thought.

steps.title: Fragment
steps.prompt: Which is a fragment?
steps.feedback: Yes. It starts an idea but does not finish it.
steps.hint: Ask whether the thought feels complete.

steps.title: Run-On
steps.prompt: Which sentence is a run-on?
choices: The rain stopped we went outside.
The rain stopped, so we went outside.
After the rain stopped, we went outside.
steps.correctAnswer: The rain stopped we went outside.
steps.feedback: Correct. Two complete ideas are pushed together without proper joining.
steps.hint: Look for two sentences stuck together.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A fragment can be corrected by adding the missing subject or predicate.
steps.feedback: Correct. Add what is missing to complete the thought.
steps.hint: Fragments are missing something important.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised spotting complete sentences and sentence problems.

steps.title: Choose a Clear Correction
steps.prompt: Fix without changing the meaning
steps.text: When you fix a fragment or run-on, keep the intended meaning. You may add missing words, use a period, use a comma with a joining word, or rewrite the sentence more clearly.

steps.title: Fix a Fragment
steps.prompt: Which best fixes the fragment 'While the soup simmered on the stove'?
choices: While the soup simmered on the stove, Dad sliced bread.
While the soup simmered on the stove.
The soup while simmered on the stove.
steps.correctAnswer: While the soup simmered on the stove, Dad sliced bread.
steps.feedback: Correct. It completes the thought.
steps.hint: The word while starts an idea that needs finishing.

steps.title: Fix a Run-On
steps.prompt: Which best fixes 'The wind rose the branches shook'?
choices: The wind rose, and the branches shook.
The wind rose the, branches shook.
The wind rose and the branches.
steps.correctAnswer: The wind rose, and the branches shook.
steps.feedback: Yes. The comma and and join two complete ideas.
steps.hint: Use punctuation and a joining word.

steps.title: Best Punctuation
steps.prompt: Which correction is clearest?
choices: I packed my lunch. Then I filled my water bottle.
I packed my lunch then I filled my water bottle.
steps.correctAnswer: I packed my lunch. Then I filled my water bottle.
steps.feedback: Correct. Two clear sentences work well here.
steps.hint: A period can separate complete thoughts.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Every long sentence is a run-on.
steps.feedback: Correct. A long sentence can be correct if it is joined and punctuated properly.
steps.hint: Length alone is not the problem.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised fixing sentence problems.

quiz.title: Complete Sentences, Fragments, and Run-Ons Quiz

questions.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
choices: The hikers reached the lookout before sunset.
questions.correctAnswer: The hikers reached the lookout before sunset.

questions.prompt: Which is a fragment?
choices: The dog slept under the wooden bench.
questions.reviewNote: It does not say what is under the bench.

questions.prompt: Which is a run-on?
choices: The timer rang we removed the muffins.
The timer rang, and we removed the muffins.
When the timer rang, we removed the muffins.
questions.correctAnswer: The timer rang we removed the muffins.
questions.reviewNote: Two complete ideas are joined incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Which best fixes 'Because the road was icy'?
choices: Because the road was icy, the bus drove slowly.
questions.correctAnswer: Because the road was icy, the bus drove slowly.

questions.prompt: Which best fixes 'The lights flickered the room went dark'?
choices: The lights flickered, and the room went dark.
The lights flickered the, room went dark.
The lights flickered and the room.
questions.correctAnswer: The lights flickered, and the room went dark.

questions.prompt: In 'The little boat rocked gently,' what is the subject?
questions.reviewNote: The subject tells what the sentence is about.

questions.type: A complete sentence needs to express a complete thought.
A run-on can sometimes be fixed by making two separate sentences.
questions.correctAnswer: A period can separate complete ideas.

lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise recognizing sentence boundaries and correcting common sentence errors.

lessons.title: Combining Sentences with Conjunctions
lessons.learningGoal: Students will combine related ideas using conjunctions and punctuation.
successCriteria: I can choose a conjunction that shows the right relationship.
I can combine sentences without creating a run-on.
I can use commas correctly in common compound sentences.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise combining related ideas with conjunctions such as and, but, so, because, although, and while.
lessonContent: A conjunction joins words, phrases, or clauses and shows how ideas are related.
And adds a related idea. But shows contrast. So shows a result. Because gives a reason.
Although and while can begin an idea that needs to be completed by the rest of the sentence.
When two complete sentences are joined with and, but, or so, a comma often comes before the conjunction.
Combining sentences should make the writing clearer, not just longer.

Use the lesson quiz as a scored check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Language lesson.

studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Conjunction meanings, compound sentences, and clear sentence combining

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided practice and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Sentence Connector Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose the best joining word and punctuation for related ideas.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: joining words show relationships
steps.text: Conjunctions help readers understand how ideas connect. Use and to add, but to contrast, so to show a result, and because to give a reason.

steps.title: Choose by Meaning
steps.prompt: Ask how the ideas connect
steps.text: Before choosing a conjunction, decide the relationship between the ideas. If the second idea is surprising, but may fit. If the second idea happens because of the first, so may fit. If one idea explains why, because may fit. Good sentence combining keeps the meaning clear.

steps.title: Show Contrast
steps.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence? 'The trail was muddy, ____ the hikers continued carefully.'
steps.feedback: Correct. But shows contrast between muddy conditions and continuing.
steps.hint: The second idea is different from what you might expect.

steps.title: Show Reason
steps.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence? 'We brought extra pencils ____ several students forgot theirs.'
steps.feedback: Yes. Because gives the reason.
steps.hint: Ask why extra pencils were brought.

steps.title: Show Result
steps.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence? 'The battery was low, ____ we plugged in the tablet.'
steps.feedback: Correct. So shows the result.
steps.hint: The second idea happens because of the first.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: The conjunction but usually signals a contrast.
steps.feedback: Correct. But often shows a different or surprising idea.
steps.hint: Think of contrast.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing joining words.

steps.title: Punctuation Matters
steps.prompt: Join ideas carefully
steps.text: When two complete sentences are joined with and, but, or so, writers often use a comma before the conjunction. The punctuation helps readers see where one idea ends and the next begins.

steps.title: Best Combination
steps.prompt: Which combines the ideas clearly? 'The sky darkened. The team packed up the equipment.'
choices: The sky darkened, so the team packed up the equipment.
The sky darkened the team packed up the equipment.
The sky darkened because, the team packed up.
steps.correctAnswer: The sky darkened, so the team packed up the equipment.
steps.feedback: Correct. So shows the result and the comma helps separate the ideas.
steps.hint: Choose the sentence that is clear and correctly joined.

steps.title: Avoid a Run-On
steps.prompt: Which sentence is correctly joined?
choices: I finished the chapter, and I wrote a summary.
I finished the chapter and, I wrote a summary.
I finished the chapter I wrote a summary.
steps.correctAnswer: I finished the chapter, and I wrote a summary.
steps.feedback: Yes. The comma and and join the ideas clearly.
steps.hint: Avoid pushing two sentences together.

steps.title: Subordinating Conjunction
steps.prompt: Which sentence uses because clearly?
choices: Because the instructions changed, we reread the first step.
The instructions because changed we reread.
steps.correctAnswer: Because the instructions changed, we reread the first step.
steps.feedback: Correct. The because phrase is completed by the main idea.
steps.hint: Because starts a reason that needs a complete thought.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Combining sentences should keep the meaning clear, not just make the sentence longer.
steps.feedback: Correct. Combining should improve clarity.
steps.hint: Longer is not always better.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised combining sentences clearly.

questions.prompt: Which conjunction adds a related idea?
Which conjunction best fits? 'The book was long, ____ it was interesting.'
Which conjunction best fits? 'We waited inside ____ the rain was heavy.'
Which conjunction best fits? 'The lid was loose, ____ the water spilled.'
Which sentence is correctly combined?
choices: The bell rang, and the students opened their books.
The bell rang and, the students opened their books.
The bell rang the students opened their books.
questions.correctAnswer: The bell rang, and the students opened their books.
questions.reviewNote: The comma and conjunction join two complete ideas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is clearest?
choices: Although the problem was difficult, Jonah kept working.
The problem although difficult Jonah kept.
questions.correctAnswer: Although the problem was difficult, Jonah kept working.

questions.type: So can show that the second idea is a result of the first idea.
A sentence is better simply because it is longer.

lessons.title: Punctuation, Dialogue, and Commas
lessons.learningGoal: Students will use commas, quotation marks, and end punctuation to clarify meaning.
successCriteria: I can choose punctuation that matches the sentence meaning.
I can recognize correctly punctuated dialogue.
I can use commas in lists, introductory phrases, and compound sentences.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise punctuation choices that help readers understand pauses, lists, speech, and sentence boundaries.
lessonContent: Punctuation is part of meaning because it shows readers where to pause, stop, ask, connect, or show speech.
Commas can separate items in a list, follow introductory words or phrases, and help join two complete ideas.
End punctuation shows whether a sentence is a statement, command, question, or exclamation.
Quotation marks go around the exact words a person says.
In dialogue, the punctuation for the spoken words usually stays inside the quotation marks.

studentActivity.title: Punctuation Patrol
studentActivity.mission: Choose punctuation that makes sentences clear and easy to read.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: punctuation guides readers
steps.text: Punctuation is not decoration. It tells readers where ideas pause, stop, connect, or show speech. A small mark can change how a sentence is understood.

steps.title: Three Common Comma Jobs
steps.prompt: Use commas to guide the reader
steps.text: Commas often do three useful jobs in Grade 5 writing. They separate items in a list: 'paper, pencils, and glue.' They follow an opening phrase: 'After lunch, we cleaned up.' They can help join two complete ideas: 'The rain stopped, and we went outside.'

steps.title: Comma in a List
steps.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
choices: We packed water, snacks, maps, and jackets.
We packed water snacks, maps and, jackets.
We packed, water snacks maps and jackets.
steps.correctAnswer: We packed water, snacks, maps, and jackets.
steps.feedback: Correct. Commas separate the items in the list.
steps.hint: Look for the sentence where each item is clear.

steps.title: Introductory Phrase
steps.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: After the storm, the streets were quiet.
After, the storm the streets were quiet.
After the storm the, streets were quiet.
steps.correctAnswer: After the storm, the streets were quiet.
steps.feedback: Yes. The comma follows the introductory phrase.
steps.hint: The first phrase sets up when.

steps.title: End Punctuation
steps.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark?
choices: Where did you put the library book
Please put the book on the shelf
The book is on the table
steps.correctAnswer: Where did you put the library book
steps.feedback: Correct. It asks a question.
steps.hint: Questions need question marks.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A comma can help separate two complete ideas joined by and, but, or so.
steps.feedback: Correct. This is common in compound sentences.
steps.hint: Think of two sentences joined together.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised commas and end punctuation.

steps.title: Punctuate Speech
steps.prompt: Show exactly what was said
steps.text: Dialogue uses quotation marks around the spoken words. The comma, question mark, or exclamation mark usually goes inside the closing quotation mark.

steps.title: Quotation Marks
steps.prompt: Which sentence punctuates dialogue correctly?
choices: Lena said, "I found the missing page."
"Lena said, I found the missing page."
Lena said, I found "the missing page."
steps.correctAnswer: Lena said, "I found the missing page."
steps.feedback: Correct. The spoken words are inside quotation marks.
steps.hint: Only the words spoken go inside quotation marks.

steps.title: Question in Dialogue
steps.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
steps.feedback: Yes. The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks.
steps.hint: The spoken question is inside the quotation marks.

steps.title: Speaker Tag
steps.prompt: What is the speaker tag in this sentence? "I can help," said Priya.
steps.feedback: Correct. The speaker tag tells who spoke.
steps.hint: Look for the part outside the quotation marks that names the speaker.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Quotation marks show the exact words a person says.
steps.feedback: Correct. Quotation marks mark spoken words.
steps.hint: They show direct speech.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised punctuation and dialogue.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
choices: The garden had beans, carrots, lettuce, and peas.
The garden had beans carrots, lettuce and, peas.
The garden, had beans carrots lettuce and peas.
questions.correctAnswer: The garden had beans, carrots, lettuce, and peas.
questions.reviewNote: Commas separate items in a list.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Before dinner, we washed the vegetables.
Before, dinner we washed the vegetables.
Before dinner we, washed the vegetables.
questions.correctAnswer: Before dinner, we washed the vegetables.
questions.reviewNote: The comma follows the introductory phrase.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
choices: The snow melted, and the path became muddy.
The snow melted and, the path became muddy.
The snow melted the path became muddy.
questions.correctAnswer: The snow melted, and the path became muddy.
questions.reviewNote: The comma and and join two complete ideas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark?
Which sentence is correct?
choices: The bus is here," called Omar.
questions.reviewNote: The spoken words are inside quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
choices: "May I borrow a ruler?" asked Grace.
"May I borrow a ruler"? asked Grace.
May I borrow a ruler? "asked Grace."
questions.correctAnswer: "May I borrow a ruler?" asked Grace.
questions.reviewNote: The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks.

questions.type: A speaker tag tells who said the words.
Punctuation can change how clearly a sentence is understood.

lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise punctuation choices that help readers understand pauses, lists, speech, and sentence boundaries.

lessons.title: Editing for Clarity and Style
lessons.learningGoal: Students will revise sentences to improve clarity, precision, grammar, and style.
successCriteria: I can choose a clearer revision.
I can remove unnecessary repetition.
I can keep the meaning while improving grammar and word choice.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise choosing revisions that improve clarity without changing the intended meaning.
lessonContent: Revision improves ideas, order, sentence flow, and word choice.
Editing checks grammar, punctuation, capitalization, and spelling.
A clear revision keeps the intended meaning while making the sentence easier to understand.
Precise nouns and verbs often make writing stronger than general words.
Writers should watch for repeated ideas, unclear pronouns, awkward word order, and descriptions that are too far away from the words they describe.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as a scored check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Language lesson.

studentActivity.title: Clear Sentence Editor
studentActivity.mission: Choose revisions that make writing clearer and more precise.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: make writing clearer
steps.text: Editing is not only finding mistakes. Writers also revise sentences so the meaning is clearer, the words are more precise, and the sentence sounds smoother.

steps.title: Revision Choices
steps.prompt: Improve without changing the idea
steps.text: A good revision does not simply make a sentence longer. It keeps the meaning and makes it clearer. Specific nouns and verbs help: 'The squirrel scampered' is clearer than 'The animal went.' Removing repeated ideas also helps the sentence sound stronger.

steps.title: Precise Word
steps.prompt: Which revision is clearest? 'The animal moved across the yard.'
choices: The squirrel scampered across the yard.
The thing went across the yard.
The animal did movement across the yard.
steps.correctAnswer: The squirrel scampered across the yard.
steps.feedback: Correct. Squirrel and scampered are more precise.
steps.hint: Choose specific nouns and verbs.

steps.title: Remove Repetition
steps.prompt: Which sentence avoids unnecessary repetition?
choices: The bright lantern glowed beside the tent.
The bright lantern was bright beside the tent.
The lantern glowed with glowing light beside the tent.
steps.correctAnswer: The bright lantern glowed beside the tent.
steps.feedback: Yes. It is clear without repeating the same idea.
steps.hint: Avoid saying the same idea twice.

steps.title: Tone
steps.prompt: Which sentence sounds most appropriate for a school report?
choices: The experiment showed that salt dissolved faster in warm water.
The salt thing did stuff in the water.
Warm water was super awesome with salt.
steps.correctAnswer: The experiment showed that salt dissolved faster in warm water.
steps.feedback: Correct. It is clear and appropriate for a report.
steps.hint: A school report needs precise, respectful wording.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Precise words can help readers picture the meaning more clearly.
steps.feedback: Correct. Specific words help readers understand.
steps.hint: Precise writing reduces guessing.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised improving word choice.

steps.title: Keep the Meaning
steps.prompt: Improve without changing the idea
steps.text: A good revision keeps the writer's intended meaning while making the sentence clearer. Watch for confusing pronouns, missing information, awkward order, and repeated words.

steps.title: Clear Pronoun
steps.prompt: Which revision is clearest? 'Emma told Zoe she had won the contest.'
choices: Emma told Zoe, "You won the contest."
Emma told Zoe she had won.
She told her about the contest.
steps.correctAnswer: Emma told Zoe, "You won the contest."
steps.feedback: Correct. This makes it clear that Zoe won.
steps.hint: The original pronoun she is unclear.

steps.title: Awkward Order
steps.prompt: Which revision is clearest? 'With a cracked handle, Noah carried the mug carefully.'
choices: Noah carefully carried the mug with a cracked handle.
With a cracked handle, carefully Noah carried.
The cracked handle carefully carried Noah's mug.
steps.correctAnswer: Noah carefully carried the mug with a cracked handle.
steps.feedback: Yes. The revision makes clear that the mug has the cracked handle.
steps.hint: Place describing words near what they describe.

steps.title: Combine Ideas
steps.prompt: Which revision is smoothest? 'The room was cold. The window was open.'
choices: The room was cold because the window was open.
The room was cold the window open.
The open room was window cold.
steps.correctAnswer: The room was cold because the window was open.
steps.feedback: Correct. It connects the reason clearly.
steps.hint: Use a joining word that shows the relationship.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A revision should improve clarity while keeping the intended meaning.
steps.feedback: Correct. Revision should not accidentally change the idea.
steps.hint: Writers revise to make meaning clearer.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised editing for clarity and style.

quiz.title: Editing for Clarity and Style Quiz

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the most precise verb?
choices: The eagle soared above the cliffs.
The eagle went above the cliffs.
The eagle did above the cliffs.
questions.correctAnswer: The eagle soared above the cliffs.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids unnecessary repetition?
choices: The cold wind rattled the windows.
The cold wind was cold and windy.
The wind blew with windy wind.
questions.correctAnswer: The cold wind rattled the windows.
questions.reviewNote: It is clear without repeating ideas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best fits a science report?
choices: The seed sprouted after six days.
The seed was doing its little thing.
questions.correctAnswer: The seed sprouted after six days.
questions.reviewNote: It is clear and appropriate for a report.

questions.prompt: Which revision is clearest? 'Mia gave Ava her notebook.'
Which sentence is clearest?
choices: The student wearing a red scarf carried the books.
Wearing a red scarf, the books were carried by the student.
The books wearing a red scarf were carried.
questions.correctAnswer: The student wearing a red scarf carried the books.

questions.prompt: Which revision connects the ideas best? 'The game was cancelled. The field was flooded.'
choices: The game was cancelled because the field was flooded.
The game was cancelled the field was flooded.
The flooded game was field cancelled.
questions.correctAnswer: The game was cancelled because the field was flooded.

questions.type: Revision can improve word choice and sentence order.
Editing should make a sentence confusing so readers have to work harder.

lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise choosing revisions that improve clarity without changing the intended meaning.

quiz.title: Vocabulary, Grammar, and Sentence Skills Unit Quiz

questions.prompt: The instructions were brief, only three short steps. What does brief mean?
questions.reviewNote: Only three short steps gives the clue.

questions.prompt: Unlike the crowded hallway, the office was spacious. What does spacious mean?
questions.reviewNote: Unlike crowded gives a contrast clue.

questions.prompt: What does the prefix un- mean in unfamiliar?
Which word means without harm?
In 'The careful gardener watered the seedlings gently,' which word is an adverb?
questions.reviewNote: Gently tells how the gardener watered.

questions.prompt: In 'The backpack is beside the desk,' which word is a preposition?
Which sentence is clearest?
choices: After Liam helped Ethan, Liam packed his bag.
After Liam helped Ethan, he packed his bag.
After he helped him, his bag was packed.
questions.correctAnswer: After Liam helped Ethan, Liam packed his bag.

questions.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
choices: The class measured the plant each Friday.
questions.correctAnswer: The class measured the plant each Friday.

questions.prompt: Which is a fragment?
questions.reviewNote: It starts an idea but does not finish it.

questions.prompt: Which is a run-on?
choices: The lights dimmed the play began.
The lights dimmed, and the play began.
When the lights dimmed, the play began.
questions.correctAnswer: The lights dimmed the play began.
questions.reviewNote: Two complete ideas are pushed together.

questions.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence? 'The road was closed, ____ we took a different route.'
Which word best completes the sentence? 'The work was challenging, ____ the group finished it carefully.'
Which sentence uses commas correctly?
choices: We need paper, markers, scissors, and glue.
We need paper markers, scissors and, glue.
We need, paper markers scissors and glue.
questions.correctAnswer: We need paper, markers, scissors, and glue.

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates dialogue correctly?
choices: Please pass the ruler," said Ben.
questions.reviewNote: The spoken words are in quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark?
choices: Why did the magnet stick to the nail
The magnet stuck to the nail
Put the magnet beside the nail
questions.correctAnswer: Why did the magnet stick to the nail

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the most precise verb?
choices: The fox crept through the grass.
The fox went through the grass.
The fox did through the grass.
questions.correctAnswer: The fox crept through the grass.

questions.prompt: Which revision is clearest? 'The backpack beside the lunch bag with the blue zipper is mine.'
choices: The backpack with the blue zipper beside the lunch bag is mine.
Beside the lunch bag mine is the backpack zipper.
The lunch bag with mine is beside the blue backpack.
questions.correctAnswer: The backpack with the blue zipper beside the lunch bag is mine.
questions.reviewNote: The describing phrase is placed more clearly.

questions.type: Good editing should make writing clearer while keeping the intended meaning.
questions.correctAnswer: Editing should improve clarity without changing the idea.
